subject: ent
title: Facial Nerve Course, Intratemporal Branches, and Bell Palsy

steps.tx: The facial nerve (cranial nerve seven) possesses a complex anatomical trajectory divided into intracranial, intratemporal, and extracranial segments. Departing the caudal border of the pons at the cerebellopontine angle, the motor root and sensory nervus intermedius traverse the internal acoustic meatus alongside the vestibulocochlear nerve. The **intratemporal segment** measures roughly thirty millimetres within the petrous temporal bone, coursing through the fallopian canal from meatus to stylomastoid foramen.
steps.say: The facial nerve traverses intracranial, intratemporal, and extracranial segments. Its thirty-millimetre intratemporal path runs inside the fallopian canal of the petrous temporal bone.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing the course of the facial nerve from brainstem to facial muscles
vis.caption: Anatomical course of the facial nerve through the temporal bone and its peripheral motor branches. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Within the temporal bone, the fallopian canal is subdivided into three consecutive anatomical segments. The narrowest and shortest is the labyrinthine segment (measuring three to four millimetres in length and only zero point six millimetres in caliber). Because of this tight bony bottleneck, inflammatory edema in the **labyrinthine segment** easily strangulates axonal blood supply, making it the principal anatomical site of compression in Bell palsy.
steps.say: The labyrinthine segment is the shortest and narrowest part of the fallopian canal. Measuring only zero point six millimetres, it is the primary site of ischemic strangulation in Bell palsy.

vis.title: Intratemporal Segments of the Fallopian Canal
rows: Runs above oval window and promontory

steps.tx: At the first genu, the nerve expands into the sensory geniculate ganglion and gives off its first intratemporal branch, the greater superficial petrosal nerve. Traversing the hiatus of the facial canal, this nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres across the middle cranial fossa to synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion, governing **lacrimal gland secretion** and seromucinous glands of the nasal mucosa and palate.
steps.say: Arising at the geniculate ganglion, the greater superficial petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion to control tearing and nasal secretion.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram of facial nerve branches, geniculate ganglion, and parasympathetic pathways
vis.caption: Intratemporal branches of the facial nerve: greater petrosal, nerve to stapedius, and chorda tympani. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The tympanic segment passes horizontally along the medial wall of the middle ear above the promontory and oval window. After rounding the second genu inferior to the lateral semicircular canal, the vertical mastoid segment gives off the **nerve to stapedius**, which enters the pyramidal eminence to innervate the stapedius muscle. Loss of this acoustic reflex dampening produces hyperacusis, where everyday environmental sounds sound painfully loud.
steps.say: In the vertical segment, the nerve to stapedius arises to innervate the stapedius muscle. Paralysis eliminates middle ear sound damping, producing painful hyperacusis.

left.title: Nerve to Stapedius Intact
points: Acoustic reflex triggers bilateral stapedial contraction.
Stiffens ossicular chain against loud sounds (>70 dB).
Protects cochlear hair cells from acoustic trauma.
Normal tolerance to everyday sound volumes.

right.title: Nerve to Stapedius Paralyzed
points: Loss of ossicular acoustic impedance damping.
Everyday moderate sounds feel uncomfortably loud.
Classic symptom of hyperacusis in Bell palsy.

steps.tx: Roughly six millimetres above the stylomastoid foramen, the mastoid segment yields the **chorda tympani nerve**. It arches upward across the posterior middle ear wall, traversing the tympanic membrane between the incus long process and malleus neck before exiting through the petrotympanic fissure. It carries special sensory taste fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.
steps.say: The chorda tympani crosses the eardrum between incus and malleus. It carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and secretomotor fibres to submandibular glands.

steps.tx: Bell palsy is the most common cause of acute, spontaneous, isolated lower motor neuron facial paralysis, accounting for three-quarters of all clinical cases. Current molecular evidence implicates viral reactivation of **herpes simplex virus type 1** within the geniculate ganglion. Viral reactivation incites perineural inflammation, microvascular ischemia, and secondary mechanical entrapment within the rigid, unyielding confines of the labyrinthine segment.
steps.say: Bell palsy is an acute lower motor neuron weakness caused by herpes simplex virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, leading to inflammatory edema and nerve strangulation.

nodes.label: Inflammatory Edema in Narrow Labyrinthine Canal

steps.tx: Patients present with sudden unilateral facial paralysis that evolves over twenty-four to seventy-two hours, characterized by loss of forehead wrinkling, inability to close the eye (**lagophthalmos**), flattening of the nasolabial fold, and sagging of the oral commissure with saliva drooling. Attempting eye closure causes the globe to roll upward and outward, an involuntary physiological phenomenon designated Bell phenomenon.
steps.say: Bell palsy causes loss of forehead wrinkles, mouth drooping, and incomplete eye closure. Attempting eye closure rolls the eyeball upward and outward in Bell phenomenon.

vis.title: Differentiating Lower Versus Upper Motor Neuron Facial Palsy
rows: Marked oral angle drooping and drooling
Hyperacusis, loss of taste, reduced tears

steps.tx: Ramsay Hunt syndrome, or herpes zoster oticus, is caused by reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion. It presents with a severe neuralgic earache followed by painful herpetic vesicles over the concha, external auditory canal, and anterior tongue, coupled with acute lower motor neuron facial palsy. Because inflammation spills into the eighth nerve, patients suffer **sensorineural hearing loss** and severe vertigo.
steps.say: Ramsay Hunt syndrome stems from varicella zoster reactivation. It produces severe ear pain, conchal blisters, facial palsy, vertigo, and sensorineural hearing loss.

right.title: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome (VZV)
points: Painful herpetic vesicles on concha and ear canal.
Associated SNHL, tinnitus, and severe vertigo.
Much more intense, burning neuralgic otalgia.
